strengths: GIQ targets an important and underexplored capability: fine-grained 3D geometric understanding beyond performance on conventional recognition benchmarks.
The collection is distinctive, covering many polyhedral families and pairing controlled synthetic renderings with unusually labor-intensive photographs of physical paper models.

The paper evaluates several complementary capabilities—reconstruction, symmetry detection, viewpoint-invariant matching, and vision-language classification—across a broad selection of contemporary models.
The symmetry results provide useful evidence that DINOv2 features transfer comparatively well from synthetic to real imagery, and the qualitative examples clearly expose recurring VLM errors.
weaknesses: The monocular reconstruction study is far too limited to support its central conclusions: it evaluates only three shapes under two image conditions, reports qualitative examples only, and omits standard mesh metrics such as Chamfer distance, F-score, normal consistency, or IoU despite having geometric ground truth.

The mental-rotation protocol is insufficiently specified and potentially problematic. The hard pairs are manually selected, Figure 2 describes accuracy specifically on negative pairs, and the paper does not report class composition, shape-disjoint splitting, sample counts, variance, or whether near-duplicate views leak across train and test. Under an all-negative evaluation, the stated 50% chance baseline would not be justified. Moreover, training and testing on synthetic-wild pairs does not demonstrate the claimed cross-domain generalization.

The symmetry probe does not establish genuine 3D reasoning. Object-level symmetry labels may be predicted from category-correlated silhouettes or local image cues, and no controls test this alternative explanation. The axis convention, annotation procedure, dataset sizes, hyperparameters, repeated-run variance, and per-shape results are also missing.

The zero-shot name-classification task conflates geometric reasoning with memorization of highly specialized polyhedron nomenclature. There is no human baseline, constrained-choice or property-level evaluation, prompt sensitivity analysis, repeated sampling, exact-match scoring specification, uncertainty estimate, or contamination analysis. Allowing Gemini to perform web search further makes the proprietary-model comparison uncontrolled.

Dataset accounting and scope are unclear. The category counts in Table 1 sum to more than 224 because categories overlap, but membership and evaluation partitions are not precisely defined. The real-image collection covers only a subset of the listed shapes, while the abstract can be read as claiming real imagery for all 224. Important details are deferred to unavailable supplementary material.

The empirical conclusions are substantially stronger than the evidence: qualitative failures and modest linear-probe results do not justify broad claims about models' 'true understanding,' implicit encoding of fundamental 3D structure, or human-level differences without stronger controls and human performance measurements.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a benchmark submission: model checkpoint/API versions, decoding settings, preprocessing details, training schedules, seeds, confidence intervals, complete prompts, and machine-readable split definitions are not provided in the manuscript. The nominal public-release link is also absent in the supplied version.

There are multiple presentation-quality issues, including the incomplete sentence describing who constructed the physical models, an incorrect reference to 'Table 3b' rather than Figure 3b, minor grammatical errors, and unclear terminology such as the relationship among overlapping stellation, compound, Kepler-Poinsot, and uniform non-convex categories.

strengths: GIQ targets an important and relatively underexplored question: whether vision foundation models encode precise 3D geometry rather than merely category and appearance cues.
The collection is visually impressive and potentially useful, combining controlled renderings with photographs of carefully constructed physical polyhedra across diverse backgrounds and viewpoints.
The benchmark covers a broad range of polyhedra, including difficult nonconvex, stellated, and compound shapes, with exact mathematical properties that can support controlled analysis.
The experiments span complementary model families and tasks, and the symmetry experiment commendably evaluates transfer from synthetic training images to real photographs using held-out shapes.
Several empirical observations are interesting, particularly DINOv2's comparatively strong symmetry-probe performance and the pronounced synthetic-to-real degradation.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not sufficiently rigorous to support the paper's broad claims. Monocular reconstruction is assessed only qualitatively on three shapes, with selected front and side renderings, no geometric metric, no aggregate results, no uncertainty, and no systematic analysis over the claimed 224-shape benchmark. This makes the conclusion that current methods fail even on basic forms vulnerable to selection bias.

The Mental Rotation Test protocol is seriously underspecified and potentially invalid. Figure 2 describes accuracy on 'negative' pairs, yet interprets 50% as chance without explaining the positive-pair construction or class balance. Sample counts, split construction, shape disjointness, leakage prevention, repetitions, and uncertainty are absent. The claim that distinctions are readily apparent to humans is also unsupported by a human baseline.

The symmetry task does not cleanly establish 3D reasoning. Its labels are object-level and viewpoint-independent, so a probe can succeed by recognizing correlated shape or family cues rather than inferring symmetry from visible 3D structure. Results come from only 26 held-out shapes, with no controls, alternative splits, per-family breakdowns, confidence intervals, or tests against simpler appearance/category baselines.

Zero-shot name classification is a weak proxy for geometric reasoning because it strongly depends on exposure to specialized polyhedron terminology and images during pretraining. The paper gives no per-class sample counts, model/API versions and dates, decoding settings, repeated-run protocol, uncertainty, or contamination analysis. Allowing Gemini to perform a web search also appears inconsistent with a controlled comparison unless equivalent tool access was provided to every model.

Crucial benchmark and experimental details are deferred to supplementary material that is not present in the manuscript: dataset splits, complete MRT results, alternative embedding combinations, and additional reconstructions. Code, annotation formats, label-generation procedures, and a usable release link are not adequately documented here, substantially limiting reproducibility.

The dataset description is not fully auditable. The category counts in Table 1 sum to more than 224 because categories overlap, but the exact unique composition and overlap structure are not reported. The number of physical shapes and exact number of real images are also unclear, with only approximate per-shape counts.

There are technical and expository inaccuracies. For example, Archimedean solids are described as edge-transitive, which is not generally true, and the discussion of Catalan solids and vertex uniformity is confusing. The identity of the 'SAM' featurizer and its citations is also ambiguous.

The paper repeatedly characterizes its evaluations as comprehensive, systematic, and indicative of human-level geometric deficiencies, but the presented evidence is mostly small-scale, qualitative, or incompletely specified. The dataset itself has promise, but the current experimental validation is not competitive for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: GIQ targets an important and underexplored problem: controlled evaluation of 3D geometric understanding rather than performance on broad, potentially shortcut-prone vision benchmarks.

The collection of 224 polyhedra spans unusually diverse families, complexities, convexities, and symmetries; pairing synthetic renderings with carefully constructed physical models is a distinctive and potentially valuable resource.

The paper evaluates complementary capabilities—reconstruction, symmetry recognition, cross-domain shape matching, and vision-language classification—and the synthetic-to-real symmetry results, particularly for DINOv2, are interesting.
The manuscript is accessible and visually polished, with figures that effectively communicate the dataset’s breadth and representative model failures.
weaknesses: The central empirical support is insufficient for a benchmark paper at a top-tier venue. Reconstruction is evaluated qualitatively on only three shapes under six input conditions, without quantitative geometry metrics, aggregate results, uncertainty, or a systematic analysis across complexity levels. This does not support broad claims about current reconstruction methods.

Key protocol details are deferred to supplementary material that is not present in the manuscript. Dataset composition, exact image counts, train/validation/test splits, hyperparameters, seeds, model checkpoints, preprocessing, and annotation procedures are consequently not reproducible from the submission.

The mental-rotation experiment is underspecified and potentially problematic. The figure describes accuracy on “negative” pairs, but the construction and balance of positive and negative examples are unclear. Hard pairs are manually selected, no human baseline validates the assertion that they are readily distinguishable, and the text inconsistently frames mixed-domain training/testing as synthetic-to-real generalization.

The zero-shot classification evaluation conflates visual geometric reasoning with memorized polyhedron terminology. It lacks exact sample counts, repeated trials, confidence intervals, alias-aware scoring details, and sufficiently precise prompting/inference procedures. Allowing Gemini to perform a web search further makes the comparison uncontrolled and potentially introduces direct answer lookup.

The symmetry probes may learn shape-category or rendering cues correlated with shape-level symmetry labels rather than infer 3D symmetry. Shape-disjoint testing is helpful, but stronger controls—such as matched shapes, counterfactual renderings, viewpoint analysis, simple geometric baselines, and multiple split seeds—are needed to substantiate the claimed 3D understanding.

Dataset accounting is confusing: the category counts in Table 1 sum to more than 224 because categories overlap, while the exact membership and size of the real-image subset remain unclear. The paper also provides no meaningful analysis of annotation validation, licensing, release contents, or benchmark governance.

Several conclusions are stronger than the evidence. For example, near-chance embedding-based matching and exact-name classification failures do not by themselves establish a general lack of geometric reasoning, while successful linear probing does not establish that embeddings inherently encode a recoverable 3D representation.

The related-work positioning and technical presentation need tightening, including comparisons with more targeted geometric/spatial benchmarks and correction or clarification of ambiguous model citations and some imprecise geometric definitions. Overall, the dataset idea is promising, but major experimental and reproducibility gaps prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: GIQ targets an important and underexplored capability: precise 3D geometric reasoning rather than recognition driven primarily by texture or category cues.
The collection is conceptually well designed, covering 224 polyhedra with controlled synthetic renderings and challenging photographs of physical models across diverse geometric families.

The paper evaluates several complementary capabilities—reconstruction, symmetry prediction, mental rotation, and fine-grained classification—and includes a broad selection of vision encoders, reconstruction systems, frontier VLMs, and geometry-native models.
Shape-disjoint cross-validation for symmetry probing and synthetic-to-real evaluation are sensible choices. The mental-rotation human study also provides a useful reference point.
The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and yields interesting diagnostic findings, including strong synthetic-to-real symmetry probing but weak fine-grained discrimination.
weaknesses: The submitted PDF repeatedly defers essential results and methodological details to an appendix, but no appendix is included. Missing information includes dataset composition, split construction, quantitative reconstruction results, probe architectures and training details, hard-pair generation, ablations, and per-domain results. This substantially prevents verification and reproduction.

The monocular reconstruction evaluation is far too limited for the paper's broad claims: the main paper shows only qualitative outputs for three selected shapes, with no metrics, uncertainty, aggregate results, or systematic analysis across the advertised complexity hierarchy.

The mental-rotation protocol is underspecified. It is unclear whether the hard split is shape-disjoint, how negative pairs and visually similar distractors are constructed, how many pairs are used, and whether images or identities recur across training and test sets. Consequently, identity memorization or dataset cues cannot be excluded.

The symmetry experiment establishes decodability by supervised probes, not geometric reasoning. Because labels are object-level and correlated with polyhedron family and appearance, probes may classify shape/category cues rather than infer 3D symmetry. Relevant controls, such as matched-category evaluation, texture/background controls, and comparisons with simple supervised baselines, are absent.

Reported plots provide point estimates without fold-wise variance, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or sample counts. Differences among encoders may therefore be insignificant, especially with only 224 unique shapes.

The frontier-model evaluation lacks critical reproducibility details such as the exact number and selection of images, decoding settings, repetitions, model/API snapshots, complete prompts, and treatment of refusals. Allowing web search in at least one illustrated response also raises contamination and comparability concerns.

The comparison between supervised nonlinear probes and untrained human participants does not support a clean human–model parity claim. The human study is small—only 20 hard questions per participant—and no uncertainty for the mean or significance analysis is reported.

Several conclusions overreach the evidence. Failure on specialized polyhedron naming does not necessarily demonstrate deficient geometric reasoning, while claims that a single view is 'informationally complete' or that failure implies texture-based approximation are not established experimentally.

The benchmark's novelty and relationship to prior synthetic geometry, symmetry, and mental-rotation benchmarks are discussed only broadly; the paper does not provide a concrete comparison of annotations, scale, task coverage, or unique advantages.

There are technical and presentation issues, including the inaccurate characterization of all Archimedean solids as edge-transitive, inconsistent or ambiguous model naming/citations, blank resource attribution/link fields, and no documented release artifacts in the submission.

strengths: The central idea is relevant: controlled polyhedra provide precise geometric attributes and can expose failures hidden by conventional recognition benchmarks.
GIQ spans synthetic renderings and photographs, multiple polyhedron families, and several tasks, including reconstruction, symmetry prediction, mental rotation, and open-ended classification.
The shape-disjoint cross-validation described for symmetry probing is preferable to randomly splitting individual rendered views.
Including geometry-native models and a 42-participant human study broadens the empirical scope and produces some potentially useful observations, such as strong DINOv2 symmetry-probing performance.
weaknesses: The submission repeatedly places essential results and protocol details in an appendix, but the provided 14-page manuscript has no appendix. Missing material includes dataset composition, quantitative reconstruction results, probe comparisons, MRT construction and ablations, classification ablations, and additional examples. The dataset URL is also blank, severely limiting verification and reproducibility.

The monocular-reconstruction evidence is inadequate for the broad conclusions: the main paper evaluates only three selected shapes, principally through qualitative renderings, with no reported geometric metrics, uncertainty, systematic aggregation over shapes/views, or competitive quantitative analysis.

The mental-rotation experiment is substantially under-specified. The number and balance of pairs, negative-pair sampling, definition of the hard split, identity overlap across training and testing, probe architecture, hyperparameter selection, and uncertainty are not reported. Consequently, leakage and selection effects cannot be ruled out.

The human-model comparison is not well controlled. Models use trained probes, whereas the human familiarization/training protocol is unclear; only 20 hard questions are answered per participant; and no inferential statistics support the claimed persistent human advantage. Indeed, the best model approximately matches or slightly exceeds mean human accuracy.

Open-ended polyhedron naming primarily tests specialized taxonomy recognition and memorized visual-name associations, not necessarily geometric reasoning. The evaluation relies on manual synonym handling, gives no decoding settings or repeated trials, lacks confidence intervals and simple retrieval/supervised baselines, and even shows Gemini using Google search, confounding visual reasoning with external retrieval.

The symmetry labels are object-level properties that can often be inferred from family or identity cues rather than explicit 3D reasoning. Only three highly correlated symmetry attributes are tested, and the paper provides no controls against shortcut learning, such as texture/color interventions, adversarially matched shapes, or viewpoint-based visibility analysis.

Several claims exceed the evidence. In particular, the assertion that one view is 'informationally complete' for high-symmetry categories is unjustified, and failures on these narrow stimuli do not establish that models are broadly unprepared for complex-scene geometry or dynamics.

The geometric exposition contains technical inaccuracies: congruent regular faces alone do not define a regular polyhedron; general Archimedean solids are not edge-transitive; and translations are incorrectly included as operations mapping vertices of a finite polyhedron onto one another. These issues are concerning in a benchmark whose value depends on precise geometry.

Dataset accounting is unclear or inconsistent: the paper alternates between 224 unique shapes, overlapping group totals of 238, and an incompletely quantified subset of physical models. It does not provide an auditable shape list, per-task sample counts, annotation procedure, or validation of ground-truth labels.

Figures report point estimates without error bars, fold variability, statistical tests, or category sample counts. Overall, the benchmark concept has promise, but the submitted evidence and documentation are insufficient for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: GIQ targets an important and underexplored failure mode of foundation models: reasoning about precise 3D geometry rather than exploiting texture or category priors.

The benchmark has an appealing controlled structure, with 224 polyhedra spanning simple, complex, convex, non-convex, stellated, and compound forms and with both synthetic renderings and photographs of physical models.

The combination of synthetic-to-real evaluation, shape-disjoint cross-validation for symmetry probing, multiple vision encoders, frontier VLMs, and geometry-native models gives the study useful breadth.
The physical data collection under varied indoor and outdoor conditions is a substantial effort and makes the benchmark more valuable than a purely rendered dataset.
The mental-rotation experiment includes a human study with 42 participants, providing an informative reference point beyond model-to-model comparison.
The results reveal interesting patterns, including strong synthetic-to-real symmetry detection by DINOv2 and pronounced failures on fine-grained shape discrimination and reconstruction.
weaknesses: The submitted PDF repeatedly defers essential evidence to an appendix that is not included. Dataset composition, nonlinear-probe results, split construction, quantitative reconstruction results, prompting ablations, and many per-domain results therefore cannot be assessed.

The monocular reconstruction evaluation is especially weak: the main paper shows only qualitative results for three selected shapes and provides neither aggregate metrics nor uncertainty. This is insufficient to support broad claims about performance across the benchmark.

The mental-rotation protocol is underspecified. The paper does not adequately explain hard-negative construction, the number of training and test pairs, whether shapes and source images are disjoint across splits, class balance, probe architecture, hyperparameters, or model-selection procedures. Leakage and sensitivity to pair construction consequently cannot be ruled out.

Comparing a supervised nonlinear probe with untrained human participants does not directly establish comparable geometric reasoning. Statistical uncertainty for the model estimates and significance tests against the human results are also absent.

Exact naming of obscure polyhedra conflates geometric reasoning with factual knowledge of a specialized nomenclature. Property-based questions or recognition from a supplied candidate set would more cleanly test geometric competence.

The zero-shot VLM evaluation lacks crucial reproducibility details, including sample counts per category, repeated-run variability, decoding and API settings, exact multimodal prompts, and treatment of external tool use. One displayed Gemini response explicitly reports a Google search, which compromises the interpretation as a controlled zero-shot evaluation.

Several conclusions are stronger than the evidence. In particular, the claim that a single view is 'informationally complete' for high-symmetry categories is generally unjustified, and failure on GIQ does not by itself show that models are unprepared for complex real-world geometry or dynamics.

The benchmark's real-image coverage and total image counts are not reported precisely, and the manuscript does not document annotation validation, mesh provenance/licensing, or quality-control procedures sufficiently for a dataset contribution.

The benchmark appears promising and potentially publishable, but the missing supplementary material and incomplete quantitative evaluation prevent the current submission from providing the convincing, reproducible evidence required for an above-threshold score.
